title: When to Bring In a Local Property Manager
short: When to Bring In a Local Manager
section: Part One · Module 6 - Building Your Dream Team

slides.title: Pick the lightest local help that covers emergencies and still pays in a bad year
slides.subtitle: Lesson 6.5. When to Bring In a Local Property Manager
meta: Education only. Not legal, licensing, or insurance advice.
slides.notes:
This lesson answers one question: how much local help does a unit need, and what does that help cost you?

There are four setups. Cleaner only. Cleaner plus an on-call vendor. A co-host. Or a full manager. By the end you'll be able to pick one for a specific unit. You'll compare each one's cost against the net cash flow it leaves you, in both the base case and the stress case. The base case is a normal year. The stress case is a bad one: the nightly rate down 12% to $180 and only 60% of nights booked.

You'll also leave with a contract and vetting checklist. And you'll know which Airbnb permissions to give a co-host, and which controls you keep no matter who you hire.

We'll run Alder Street through all four setups with real math. Laid side by side, one of the four takes the whole margin. I'll show you which one, and why.

slides.title: Your cleaner covers the scheduled work; the gap is unscheduled work at odd hours
rows: Emergencies: leak, lockout, alarm, no heat
Within an hour or two, any time
slides.caption: Turnovers: 255 booked nights ÷ 3-night average stay = 85 stays a year, or about 7.1 a month (hypothetical Alder Street example).
slides.notes:
Remote operation works because most of the business is digital. Pricing, messaging, bookkeeping, and listing changes happen from anywhere. But some jobs need someone who can physically reach the unit.

Start with turnovers. A turnover is the clean between one guest's checkout and the next check-in. Alder Street books 255 nights a year at a 3-night average stay. That's 85 stays a year, or about 7.1 cleans a month. Your cleaner handles those, plus restocks if you pay them to.

Now look at the response column. The cleaner covers the scheduled work. What remote operators struggle with is the unscheduled work. The 11 p.m. lockout. The leak on a Sunday. The guest who can't get the heat on. Those need someone within an hour or two, at any time.

That's the gap local help fills. It's also exactly what you promised the landlord in the lease addendum in lesson 5.7: a named local contact who answers day and night. So this isn't optional polish. It's a commitment you've already signed.

slides.title: Each step up in local help buys back time and costs more of a thin margin

nodes.d: You run everything remotely and dispatch vendors yourself. The Alder Street base case.
Monthly retainer for set response times, a monthly inspection, and repair access
A defined share of hosting, with Airbnb permissions. Paid a percentage or fixed fee per booking.
Runs guests, cleaners, maintenance, often pricing. Usually a percentage of revenue.

box.label: The arbitrage catch
box.text: Rent is already your biggest fixed cost. Every dollar of fee comes straight out of what's left.

slides.notes:
Here are the four levels, lightest to heaviest.

Cleaner only. You run everything remotely. Your cleaner turns the unit and reports problems, and when something breaks, you find and dispatch a vendor yourself. That's the Alder Street base case. It works if you live within reach, or if you're very good at remote dispatch and the unit is simple.

Cleaner plus an on-call vendor. You add a local handyman or small service company on a monthly retainer, a flat fee that keeps them on call. They commit to a response time, do a monthly inspection, and handle repair access. You still run guests, pricing, and the platform.

A co-host takes a defined share of the hosting: guest messages, in-person issues, cleaner coordination, sometimes pricing. On Airbnb they get permissions on your listing. You pay a percentage or a fixed amount per booking.

A full manager runs the whole operation. You approve the budget and review performance. Fees are usually a percentage of revenue.

Each step up saves you more time. Each step up also costs more. In arbitrage you lease the unit, so rent is already your biggest fixed cost. Every dollar of fee comes straight out of what's left.

slides.title: If test 4 is true, or any two of five are, you need at least an on-call vendor

gates.sub: You can't reach the unit within two hours at night (assumption)
In the last 90 days, a guest waited past your promised time for an in-person fix more than once
gates.no: True if more than one miss

gates.sub: More hours a month than planned, crowding out finding the next deal
Lease addendum, permit, or house rules require a local contact you don't have (city rules: SR.1 checklist)
gates.no: True if you lack one now

gates.sub: Adding units nearby, so help too costly for one unit may pay off across three

slides.end: Test 4, or any two true: add **at least an on-call vendor**. Test 2 or 3 still true after 90 days: move up.
slides.notes:
Use five tests. If test 4 is true, or any two tests are true, you need at least an on-call vendor. Test 4 counts on its own, because it's a promise you've already made in writing.

Distance: can you reach the unit within two hours at night? That two-hour line is an assumption. Set your own.

Missed responses: in the last 90 days, did a guest wait longer than your promised response time for an in-person fix more than once?

Your hours: are you spending more time on the unit than you planned, to the point that it crowds out finding your next deal?

Written promises: does your addendum, the city permit, or your own house rules require a local contact you don't have right now? Some cities make that a permit condition. The SR.1 compliance checklist covers your city's rules.

Volume: are you adding units nearby? Help that's too expensive for one unit may pay off across three. That's a cost test, not a risk test.

After 90 days with a vendor, re-check tests 2 and 3. If either is still true, move up a level. Hiring won't change your distance.

slides.title: Five controls stay with you no matter who you hire, because you carry the consequences
items: **Bank and payouts.** Revenue flows to your account. The helper gets paid from it.
**Platform ownership.** The listing stays in your account, with your reviews, calendar, and history.
**Compliance decisions.** Permits, tax registrations, occupancy limits, and lease duties are yours. You decide and sign.
**Pricing approval.** A helper can recommend rates. You set the floor, the ceiling, and minimum stays (pricing tools: Module 9).
**Performance review.** Monthly: occupancy, nightly rate, response times, cleaning scores, complaints. The helper reports; you judge.
slides.notes:
Local help can take tasks off your plate. Certain controls stay with you, because you carry the consequences.

You keep bank and payout ownership. Revenue lands in your account, and the helper gets paid from it, not the other way around.

You keep the platform. The listing sits in your account. If the relationship ends, you remove the helper and keep your reviews, calendar, and history.

You keep compliance decisions. A manager can remind you a permit renewal is coming. You decide and you sign.

You keep pricing approval. A helper can recommend rates or run a pricing tool, but you set the floor, the ceiling, and minimum stays. Module 9 covers pricing tools, in lessons 9.10 and 9.13. There you'll see how to set that floor and ceiling inside a pricing tool, which is where this control lives.

And you keep performance review. Every month, look at occupancy, nightly rate, response times, cleaning scores, and complaints. The helper reports. You judge.

slides.title: Give a co-host the least Airbnb access the job needs, and set their payouts yourself

left.head: Permissions
items: Full access: messages, calendar, transaction history, listing management
Full access can also change other co-hosts' permissions
Lower levels limit access to calendar and messaging
You can change a co-host's permissions at any time

right.head: Payouts
items: Only the listing owner sets up co-host payouts
A percentage per booking, with or without the cleaning fee, or a fixed amount
Percentage payouts are calculated from the host's earnings (your payout after Airbnb's fee)
Regional limits may apply

box.label: Responsibility doesn't transfer
box.text: The host alone chooses co-hosts and manages access, and stays responsible for a co-host's actions before removal.

slides.notes:
If you choose a co-host, set up Airbnb access deliberately.

Airbnb offers different permission levels. A co-host with full access can see messages, the calendar, and transaction history. They can manage the listing. And they can change other co-hosts' permissions. Lower levels limit access to the calendar and messaging. You can change a co-host's permissions at any time.

Give the least access the job needs. A co-host who only handles guest messages and in-person issues may not need full access. Full access includes the power to change other co-hosts' permissions, so treat it like handing over your keys.

Payouts are the second control. Airbnb says only the listing owner can set up co-host payouts. The owner picks a percentage per booking, with or without the cleaning fee, or a fixed amount. Percentage payouts are calculated from the host's earnings, which is your payout after Airbnb's fee. That basis matters, and you'll see why in the math. Regional limits may apply, so check the page for your country.

And responsibility doesn't transfer. Airbnb's terms say the host stays responsible for a co-host's actions taken before removal. If a co-host breaks a rule, the account at risk is yours.

slides.title: Pin down coverage, response times, and money terms before you sign anything
rows: "We cover the metro area" with no named zone
Days and hours, including nights and holidays
Time to acknowledge and time on site, by issue type
Percentage or flat fee, and the base it's calculated on
Whether they add a percentage to vendor bills or supplies
Dollar amount they can spend without your approval
slides.notes:
Whoever you hire, the agreement should answer twelve questions in writing. Here are the first six, and they're about coverage and money.

Service area: the exact addresses they cover. "We cover the metro area" with no named zone is a red flag.

Coverage hours: days and hours, including nights and holidays. Business hours with emergencies handled on a best-effort basis doesn't cover the gap you're hiring for.

Response targets: time to acknowledge and time on site, by type of issue. If there are no numbers, there's no promise.

Fees: the rate and the base it's calculated on. I'll show you in a minute how the same 10% can cost two different amounts depending on the base.

Markup: do they add a percentage to vendor bills or supplies? If they won't say, assume yes.

Authorization limits: the dollar amount they can spend without asking you. "As needed" means your money, their judgment.

slides.title: Backup, insurance, reporting, data, exit, and licensing complete the contract
rows: Who covers when they're sick or away
General liability and workers' compensation, with certificates
Monthly report contents and due date; photo proof of turnovers
Who holds codes, guest data, platform logins
Notice period; handback of keys, codes, and records
Long lock-in or fees to leave
Whether managing short-term rentals for others needs a license

box.label: Vet before you sign
box.text: Two references with similar units, a certificate of insurance, a sample monthly report, and the fee schedule in writing. Then ask how they'd handle a lockout at 11 p.m. on a Saturday.

slides.notes:
The other six items protect you when things go wrong.

Backup: who covers when they're sick or away? One person with no backup is a single point of failure at 2 a.m.

Insurance: their general liability and workers' compensation, with certificates. If they can't produce a certificate, stop.

Reporting: what the monthly report contains, when it's due, and photo proof of turnovers.

Data and access: who holds the codes, the guest data, and the logins. Anyone who wants your platform password instead of a co-host invitation is a red flag.

Termination: the notice period and the handback of keys, codes, and records. Watch for long lock-ins or fees to leave.

Licensing: does local law require a license to manage short-term rentals for others? If they don't know, that tells you something.

Then vet. Ask for two references with similar units, their certificate of insurance, a sample monthly report, and the fee schedule in writing. And run one test: ask how they'd handle a lockout at 11 p.m. on a Saturday. A specific answer, with names and times, is a good sign.

slides.title: Some states license people who manage rentals for others, and your tenancy adds a wrinkle
items: Tennessee licenses Vacation Lodging Services: businesses that manage, market, book, and rent units owned by others for stays of up to 14 days. Each needs a firm license and a designated agent license ([Tennessee Real Estate Commission](https://www.tn.gov/commerce/regboards/trec/license/license-how-to/vacation-lodging-service.html)).
Other states handle this under general real estate or property management licensing. Some have no specific rule.
In arbitrage you lease the unit, so the helper works for a tenant, not the owner. Whether that changes the answer depends on the state.

box.label: Confirm with
box.text: The state real estate commission or licensing board: does the helper need a license for these services, and does it matter that you're a tenant? Ask an attorney if the answer is unclear.

slides.notes:
The licensing row needs care, so I'm giving it its own slide.

Some states regulate people who manage rentals for someone else. Tennessee is one clear example. I'm not assuming you're there. It licenses what it calls Vacation Lodging Services. Those are businesses that manage, market, book, and rent units owned by others for stays of up to 14 days. Each one needs a firm license and a designated agent license. The Tennessee Real Estate Commission page has the details of each.

Other states handle this under general real estate or property management licensing. Some have no specific rule at all.

Arbitrage adds a wrinkle. You lease the unit, so your helper works for a tenant, not for the owner. Whether that changes the licensing answer depends on the state, and I'm not going to guess for you.

So confirm it. Ask the state real estate commission or licensing board whether your helper needs a license for these services. Ask specifically whether it matters that you're a tenant. If the answer is unclear, that's a question for an attorney.

slides.title: An on-call vendor costs Alder Street $2,400 a year and still leaves $818 a month
slides.side:
**Per month:** $818, down from $1,018.

Base case: 255 nights at a $205 average daily rate (ADR), 85 stays. Gross booking revenue **$61,625**: 255 × $205 = $52,275, plus 85 stays × $110 guest cleaning fee = $9,350. Costs include Airbnb's fee, utilities, supplies, insurance, software, repairs, permit, $23,400 of rent, and the cleaner.
slides.notes:
Now the numbers. Start with the Alder Street base case. It books 255 nights at a $205 average daily rate, or ADR, which is 85 stays. Gross booking revenue is $61,625. That's $52,275 of nightly revenue plus a $110 cleaning fee on each of 85 stays. Subtract Airbnb's fee, the cleaner, utilities, supplies, insurance, software, repairs, the permit, and $23,400 in rent. Net before income tax is $12,218 a year, or $1,018 a month.

Setup 1, cleaner only, adds nothing. Net stays at $1,018 a month.

Setup 2 adds an on-call vendor. I'm assuming a $150 monthly retainer that includes one inspection and on-call response. Then a $600 yearly budget for call-outs, the visits they bill on top. That's on top of the repairs reserve already in the base case. The reserve buys parts. The call-out budget pays someone to show up.

The vendor costs $2,400 a year. Net drops to $9,818, or $818 a month. You gave up $200 a month and closed the emergency gap you promised the landlord.

side_box.label: Setup 1 for comparison
side_box.text: Cleaner only (base case): added cost $0, net $12,218 a year, $1,018 a month.

slides.title: The same 10% co-host fee costs $955 more a year on gross than on host earnings
slides.side:
Host earnings = $61,625 − $9,552 Airbnb fee (15.5% in this example) = $52,073.

**On gross:** net $6,056 a year, **$505** a month.

**On host earnings:** net $7,011 a year, **$584** a month. Airbnb calculates percentage co-host payouts from host earnings ([article 3389](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/3389)).

side_box.label: In the contract
side_box.text: Write the percentage base into the agreement.

slides.notes:
Setup 3 is a co-host at 10%. And here's where the percentage base changes the fee.

First, 10% of gross booking revenue. That's $61,625 times 10%, or $6,162 rounded. Net drops to $6,056 a year, $505 a month.

Second, 10% calculated on host earnings, which is how Airbnb calculates percentage co-host payouts. Host earnings are gross minus Airbnb's host fee. In this example that fee is 15.5%, or $9,552. So host earnings are $52,073. Ten percent of that is $5,207. Net is $7,011 a year, $584 a month.

Same "10%." A $955 difference in yearly cost.

That's why the fee row in the contract checklist says to define the base. A co-host quoting 10% of gross and one quoting 10% through Airbnb's payout tool are quoting different prices. Write the base into the contract, in words.

slides.title: A full manager at 20% of gross costs $12,325, more than Alder Street's whole net

result.label: Net per year with a full manager

slides.side:
**Per month:** about −$9, down from $1,018.

In this example the 20% doesn't include paying the cleaner. That's still $95 a turnover on top.

side_box.label: Who gets paid
side_box.text: The landlord, the manager, and the cleaner all get paid. You earn nothing for your capital and risk.

slides.notes:
Setup 4 is a full manager at 20% of gross booking revenue. That rate is my assumption for this example.

The fee is $61,625 times 20%, or $12,325 a year. The base-case net is $12,218. So the fee is bigger than everything the unit makes. Net becomes negative $107 a year, about negative $9 a month.

At 20%, the manager takes the whole margin. The landlord gets paid, the manager gets paid, and the guests get a good stay. You earn nothing for your capital and risk.

And the cleaner is still paid separately. In this example the 20% doesn't include paying the cleaner, so that's still $95 a turnover on top.

That's a normal year. Next, let's see what a bad year does to all four setups.

slides.title: In a bad year, every setup except cleaner only ends the year with a loss
slides.caption: Stress case: $180 ADR, 60% of nights booked (219 nights, 73 stays), gross $47,450 including cleaning fees, net $1,548 a year. Net per month is the yearly total ÷ 12.
slides.notes:
Now run all four through the stress case. That's the bad year: a $180 rate and 60% of nights booked, which is 219 nights and 73 stays. Gross is $47,450 including cleaning fees. Net is $1,548 a year.

Cleaner only still makes $129 a month. The vendor turns that into a $71 monthly loss. The co-host loses $266 a month on gross, or $205 on host earnings. The full manager loses $662 a month.

These monthly figures are the yearly total divided by 12. A seasonal unit will make money in some months and lose it in others. What matters is where the year ends.

So in a bad year, only cleaner only stays positive. That doesn't mean you can't add help. It means you need to know how much loss your reserve can carry before you do.

slides.title: A full manager needs 70.1% occupancy to break even; the base case books 69.9%
slides.caption: Green: $205 rate. Dark: $180 stress rate. Red: full manager. Base case books 69.9% of nights; stress case 60%. Co-host on host earnings (3b): 56.8% and 65.3%.
slides.notes:
Break-even occupancy is the share of nights you must book for revenue to cover every cost, rent included. Lesson 1.3 shows the method.

At the $205 rate, cleaner only breaks even at 49.9%. Add the vendor and it's 53.8%. A co-host at 10% of gross pushes it to 58.3%. A full manager at 20% pushes it to 70.1%.

The base case books 255 of 365 nights, 69.9%. So with a full manager, Alder Street needs 70.1% just to break even. That's why the net is slightly negative. There's no cushion at all.

At the $180 stress rate it's worse. Cleaner only needs 57.1%. The vendor needs 61.6%. The co-host needs 67.0%. The full manager needs 81.0%.

Connect this back to lesson 3.4. C1 on that scorecard was the break-even cushion. Alder Street had a 20.1-point cushion there, which earned no red-flag points. With a full manager, the cushion goes negative. So rescore after you choose.

slides.title: Fees above about 10% of gross leave Alder Street under $500 a month in a good year

box.label: Two negotiating numbers
box.text: A fee of **19.8%** of gross ($12,218 ÷ $61,625) wipes out the base-case net. About **10.1%** leaves you $500 a month. ($500 is an example floor. Use your own.)

slides.notes:
Two numbers help you negotiate.

A fee of 19.8% of gross wipes out the base-case net entirely. That's $12,218 divided by $61,625. A fee of about 10.1% leaves you $500 a month. So any percentage deal above roughly 10% of gross leaves you less than $500 a month, and that's in a good year. The $500 is just an example floor. Use your own.

Now compare cost with the time you get back. I'm assuming the vendor saves you 4 hours a month, the co-host 14, and the manager 20. Those are guesses, so track your own hours.

On those hours, the vendor is $50 per hour saved, the co-host about $37, and the manager about $51. So the co-host is cheapest per hour. But it pushes the stress case negative. Cost per hour is useful, but it isn't the deciding number. The stress case is.
slides.caption: Co-host and manager cost per hour are rounded (about $37 and about $51).

slides.text: If you live far from Alder Street, pick setup 2: it covers the emergency gap and keeps $818 a month.
slides.support: Live within two hours and can answer at night? Setup 1 can work. In a bad year setup 2 turns $129 a month into a $71 loss. The $4,420 operating reserve can carry that. A co-host fits only after lower rent or comps (comparable listings) support it.
slides.notes:
So here's what I'd pick for Alder Street, and why.

If you live within two hours and can answer at night yourself, setup 1 can work. If you live far away, I'd pick setup 2, the cleaner plus an on-call vendor. It covers the emergency gap you promised the landlord in the addendum. And it keeps $818 a month in the base case.

In a bad year, it turns a $129 monthly gain into a $71 monthly loss. That's $852 over the year. The $4,420 operating reserve from lesson 1.3, two months of rent plus utilities, can carry that. It uses about a fifth of it.

A co-host becomes reasonable only after something else improves. You negotiate lower rent at renewal, or comparable listings, called comps, support a higher rate.

The full manager doesn't fit this unit's economics at 20%. That's this unit, at this rent, at these rates.

[Producer note, do not read aloud: Preston can add a real example here if he has one.]
slides.title: For Alder Street, a far-away operator should pick the cleaner plus an on-call vendor
Compare all four setups for your unit, then pick the lightest one that clears your floor

box.label: Decision rule
box.text: Choose the lightest setup that passes the threshold tests and keeps the stress-case net at or above your floor: $______ a month. If none does, fix the deal first: lower rent or better rate evidence.

slides.notes:
Your exercise is the local help decision tool, filled in for one unit.

Part A is the five threshold tests. Mark each true or false with evidence. If test 4 is true, or two or more are true, add at least an on-call vendor.

Part B is this cost comparison. Start from your own base and stress net from lesson 1.3. For each setup, write the fee terms, including the base. Subtract the yearly cost, then fill in the monthly nets. For break-even, change occupancy in your lesson 1.3 worksheet until net reads zero.

Part C is the decision rule. Choose the lightest setup that passes the tests and keeps your stress-case net at or above your floor. If none does, fix the deal first, then rescore it on your lesson 3.4 scorecard.

Part D lists the controls you keep. Parts A and D are in the written lesson.
slides.caption: Parts A (threshold tests) and D (controls you keep) are in the written lesson, section 6.5.8.

slides.title: Five checks before signing: licensing board, insurer, attorney, permit office, Airbnb
rows: State real estate commission or licensing board
Whether your helper needs a license to manage short-term rentals for others, and whether it matters that you're a tenant
Whether your STR policy covers acts of a co-host or vendor, and which certificates to require from them
The management or co-host agreement, especially termination, authorization limits, and data access
Whether your permit requires a named local contact and a response time
Co-host permission levels and payout options in your region
slides.notes:
Here's who confirms what.

The state real estate commission or licensing board confirms whether your helper needs a license to manage short-term rentals for others. Ask whether it matters that you're a tenant, because that's the arbitrage wrinkle.

Your insurance broker confirms whether your STR policy covers the acts of a co-host or vendor. Ask which certificates you should require from them, so your vetting asks for the right paper.

An attorney reviews the management or co-host agreement. I'd point them at three terms: termination, authorization limits, and data access. Those are the terms that hurt most when a relationship ends badly.

The local licensing office confirms whether your permit requires a named local contact and a response time. If it does, that's one of your threshold tests already answered.

And Airbnb's current help pages confirm the co-host permission levels and payout options in your region. Those can differ by region and can change, so check before you set anyone up.

slides.title: Decide your unit's local help setup this week
items: Answer the five threshold tests for one unit and count how many are true.
Ask two local handymen or service companies for a written retainer quote with response times.
Run the four setups through your base and stress numbers and write your monthly floor.
If you'll use a co-host, write down the permission level and payout base you'll set before you invite anyone.
slides.next: Next: Module 7, starting with lesson 7.1, Why Design Matters. Bring your Part B cost comparison. Furnishing choices change turnover time, damage risk, and nightly rate.
slides.notes:
Four things to start this week.

Answer the five threshold tests for one unit. Count the trues. That tells you whether you need help at all.

Ask two local handymen or small service companies for a written retainer quote that includes response times. Use the contract checklist to see what's missing from what they send.

Run all four setups through your own base and stress numbers, and write down your monthly floor.

And if you're going to use a co-host, decide the permission level and the payout base before you invite anyone. It's much easier to set limits at the start than to take access away later.

You've now decided who covers the unit on the ground. Module 7 turns to the unit itself, starting with lesson 7.1, Why Design Matters. Bring your Part B cost comparison. Furnishing choices change turnover time, damage risk, and nightly rate, and those feed straight back into the numbers you just ran.

slides.title: Co-host rules come from Airbnb's help center, and licensing from a state board

items.title: Airbnb Help, article 1534: What co-hosts can do
items.note: Permission levels; full access scope; hosts can change permissions

items.title: Airbnb Help, article 3264: Co-Host Additional Terms of Service
items.note: Host alone responsible for choosing and managing co-host access and for co-host actions before removal

items.title: Airbnb Help, article 3389: How co-host payouts work
items.note: Only the listing owner sets up co-host payouts; percentage or fixed; calculated on host earnings; regional limits

items.title: Tennessee Real Estate Commission: Vacation Lodging Service Licensure
items.note: Firm and designated agent licenses for managing units owned by others for stays up to 14 days

slides.notes:
Here are the sources for this lesson. I checked summaries of these official pages on 25 September 2026. Help pages change, so open the live page before you act.

Three Airbnb help pages cover co-hosting. Article 1534 explains what co-hosts can do: the permission levels, what full access includes, and that you can change permissions any time. Article 3264 is the Co-Host Additional Terms of Service. That's where Airbnb says the host alone is responsible for choosing co-hosts and managing access, and stays responsible for a co-host's actions before removal. Article 3389 explains co-host payouts: only the listing owner sets them up, the percentage or fixed options, the host-earnings basis, and regional limits.

The Tennessee Real Estate Commission page supports the licensing example: firm and designated agent licenses for Vacation Lodging Services.

The Alder Street figures come from the example unit used across this course. The vendor, co-host, break-even, fee threshold, and cost-per-hour figures were computed from it. Fee rates and hours saved are assumptions. Swap in your own quotes before you decide.
